title: I can't forgive them
seoTitle: Can't Forgive Someone Who Hurt You? What the Bible Says
description: Forgiveness isn't forgetting, excusing, trusting again, or staying quiet about abuse. What the Bible asks, and where to start when you can't forgive.
summary: When someone hurt you and you can't let it go: what forgiveness is, what it isn't, and where to begin.
askedAs: how to forgive someone who hurt you
What does the Bible say about forgiveness?
answer: Someone hurt you, maybe a parent, a spouse, a friend, or someone in the church, and you've been told to forgive. Maybe you've tried and it won't hold. Maybe you can't bring yourself to try, because forgiving feels like saying it didn't matter. It did matter. Forgiveness is not forgetting, excusing, or pretending the wound was small; it isn't trusting them again or letting them back in; and it is never silence about abuse or a crime. You can forgive and still report, still keep your distance, still refuse contact. If the person who hurt you is still a danger to you or to a child, safety comes first, and the help just below is for tonight. If you're safe, begin by telling God exactly what happened. When forgiveness comes, it means handing him the debt, because he judges rightly, instead of spending your life trying to collect it.
happening:
It may have been one night or twenty years. The memory comes back without asking: in the shower, at the holiday table, at three in the morning when you're arguing with them in your head and finally saying what you never got to say. You've prayed the words and meant them. Then the anger came back anyway, and now you carry guilt on top of the hurt, as if your trouble forgiving had become the real sin in the story.

Some wounds are a single blow, like an affair or a secret betrayed. Some are years of small cruelties from someone who was supposed to protect you. Some are made of absence, the father who never came or the mother who never really saw you, and an absence is hard to forgive in its own way, because there's no single scene to name, only a long quiet where something should have been. Some people can't forgive because the one who hurt them died before anything could be said, and some because the person they can't forgive is themselves.

The usual explanations each hold something true. Doctors and counselors will tell you that replaying an injury keeps it fresh, that long resentment wears on sleep, health, and the people closest to you, and that someone badly hurt can stay on guard long after deciding to let go, which is one reason forgiveness is rarely finished in a single decision. Your church may have told you to forgive because you've been forgiven, and Jesus said that more sharply than any preacher. The culture has its own sayings, *forgive for your own peace* and *you don't owe anyone forgiveness*, and each holds a piece of the truth.

What they leave out is the question that keeps most people stuck: if you let it go, who answers for the wrong? They also skip the distinctions that keep forgiveness from looking like surrender. Forgiveness concerns a debt, and it happens between you and God. Reconciliation concerns a relationship; it takes two people, and it asks the one who did the harm to own it and change. Trust is earned back slowly, and some people never earn it. Much of the pressure you feel comes from people who have mashed those three together.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't hurry past what was done to you. It gives the wounded a prayer book with rage in it, a command to forgive that Jesus refused to soften, and a God who says vengeance is his, so the wrong will not go unanswered. The lament comes first on purpose: the Bible lets you tell the truth before it asks you to let go.

passages.text: For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God. ... Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken. But You, O God, will bring them down to the Pit of destruction; men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days. But I will trust in You.
passages.reading: The heading gives this psalm to David, and it's the prayer of a man betrayed by someone he worshiped beside, which makes it a prayer for anyone wounded inside a church. He doesn't tidy it up. His friend's "speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart" (Psalm 55:21), and in a verse left out here David asks God to let death take them by surprise. Then comes the line so often printed on cards. In its place, the burden he casts on the Lord is the betrayal itself, the whole case against the one who did it. Anger brought to God like this isn't the opposite of forgiveness. It's often where forgiveness begins.

passages.text: Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?” Jesus answered, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times! ... Then the master summoned him and declared, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me. Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’ In anger his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed. That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.”
passages.reading: Peter thought seven times was generous. Jesus answered with a number that means stop counting, then told of a servant forgiven ten thousand talents, a debt no lifetime of work could repay, who went out and choked a fellow servant over a hundred denarii, about a hundred days' wages (Matthew 20:2). That smaller debt was real, and Jesus never calls it nothing. The servant's sin was refusal: he had the man jailed while his own pardon was still fresh. Struggling to forgive is a different thing. The ending is meant to frighten, but it's aimed at a heart set on collecting, not at a wounded one asking God for help to let go. And "from your heart" (Matthew 18:35) explains why forgiveness takes longer than saying the words.

passages.text: Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Carefully consider what is right in the eyes of everybody. If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone. Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.” ... Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
passages.reading: Paul wrote this to Christians in the capital of an empire that crucified people. Far from calling their wrongs small, he tells them to leave room for God's wrath, because repayment belongs to God. You can lay down the sword because the case is going to a better court. Keep reading. A few sentences later Paul calls the governing authority "God's servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:4). Refusing private revenge and reporting a crime to the police belong together; the second is one way God's justice works in this world. And "If it is possible on your part" (Romans 12:18) admits that peace takes two. You answer for your side, not for making a dangerous person safe.

passages.text: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” ... But Joseph replied, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God? As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people. Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” So Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them.
passages.reading: Decades after his brothers sold him, and seventeen years after he brought the family to Egypt (Genesis 47:28), they sent him word of instructions from their father that Genesis never records him giving. Joseph wept. Then he did two things we usually pull apart: he named the wrong without softening it, and he refused the seat it offered him. "Am I in the place of God?" (Genesis 50:19). He got there slowly. Years earlier, before revealing himself, he tested them (Genesis 42:15), and the last test turned on whether they would abandon Benjamin as they had once abandoned him. Only when Judah offered himself in the boy's place (Genesis 44:33) did Joseph make himself known. Forgiveness didn't rush him into trust.

passages.text: When they came to the place called The Skull, they crucified Him there, along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left. Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
passages.reading: Jesus prayed this while the men who crucified him were casting lots for his clothes. No one had apologized, and the wrong was still being done. Look at whom he addressed. He didn't tell his executioners it was all right; it was the killing of an innocent man, and Luke tells it that way. He asked his Father to forgive them. When you can't yet say *I forgive you*, his prayer may be the place to begin. Forgiveness often starts as a prayer through clenched teeth, long before it's a feeling, and the one who prayed it first knows what it costs.

whyHard:
The usual explanation for why we can't forgive is pride, and there's truth in it. A grievance can become strange company. It lets us stay in the right, and it holds a verdict in reserve for the day we might need it. Most of us have kept one warm long after it stopped protecting anyone, and the servant in Jesus' parable lives closer to home than we like to admit.

But the person who types *I can't forgive* into a search bar at midnight is usually refusing something other than mercy. They're refusing a lie that came with it: that forgiveness means saying it didn't matter, that the wrong goes uncounted, that they must go back and act as if nothing happened. They're right to refuse it. It was never the Christian teaching.

Some of that lie came from us. Churches and families have often wanted forgiveness mainly because it's quieter. It keeps the holidays calm, keeps a respected man's name clean, keeps a ministry out of the news, and lets everyone move on except the person who was hurt. When a victim is told to forgive and the one who did the harm is asked for nothing, the wounded pay for the grace and the guilty receive it free. We pastors have done this, sometimes out of real love for a congregation, and it has taught many people that Christian forgiveness is a way of making them disappear.

The sharpest critic went further. In *On the Genealogy of Morality* (1887), Friedrich Nietzsche argued that Christian forgiveness was weakness in disguise: people too powerless to take revenge renamed their powerlessness mercy and comforted themselves that God would punish their enemies later. It's a serious charge, and the church has sometimes earned it, whenever it asked the weak to forgive so the strong could stay comfortable, and whenever believers have savored the thought of their enemies' ruin. Scripture forbids that pleasure: "Do not gloat when your enemy falls" (Proverbs 24:17). Nor is the forgiveness it describes the resignation of the powerless. Joseph had Pharaoh's authority behind him when he refused to play God.

Entrusting a wrong to God differs from postponing revenge in one way: you hand him the verdict too, including the possibility that he will show mercy to someone who turns. Jonah fled from that possibility and sulked when it came, because he knew God was "a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger" (Jonah 4:2). Revenge insists on its outcome. Entrusting gives the outcome to a Judge who is both just and merciful, who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23), and who saw everything that was done to you.

The church that pressures victims to forgive fast and the culture that tells them to forgive for their own peace or not at all share an assumption: that forgiveness happens between two people, with no one else in the room. If that were so, forgiving would mean letting evil win and refusing would be the only justice left, which is why holding on can feel like loyalty to the truth. Scripture puts a third party in the room. "You see to repay it by Your hand," the psalmist prays. "The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless" (Psalm 10:14). And the same God, at the cross, bore the cost of wrongs that were not his, ours among them.

None of this is quick, and it won't feel like winning. The wound is still yours to grieve, and the memory may stay for years. What changes, slowly, is who is holding the case. Without a Judge, forgiveness is only surrender. With one, it becomes an act of faith.

thisWeek.intro: None of this has to be finished this week, and some of it shouldn't be. These are small, honest steps you can take even when you're tired. Start with whichever one fits where you are.

steps.title: If you aren't safe, start there
steps.body: If the person who hurt you is still hurting, threatening, or controlling you, or has access to a child, forgiveness isn't this week's question. Call or text one of the hotlines at the top of this page, or 911 if you're in danger now, and tell one person who can help. Forgiveness can be worked out later, from somewhere safe.

steps.title: Write down what happened
steps.body: Write the wrong down plainly, for your eyes and God's: what they did, what it cost you, what it still costs. Don't shrink it to sound more spiritual or inflate it to win the argument in your head. You can't release a debt you won't count. If the person has died, write it as a letter to them and read it aloud to God, who holds them now, and the debt with them.

steps.title: Pray it honestly
steps.body: Read Psalm 55 aloud and tell God what you want to happen to the person who hurt you; he already knows, and saying it to him is safer than rehearsing it alone. Then, once a day, pray one sentence about them. Some days it will be "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). Other days it will be *I can't, so I'm asking you to do what I can't*. Both count.

steps.title: Separate three decisions
steps.body: Write three words across a page: forgive, trust, contact. Under each, write where you honestly are. Forgiveness is between you and God; trust has to be earned; contact is decided by safety and wisdom. You may be ready for one and nowhere near the others, and seeing that plainly can lift a weight you were never meant to carry.

steps.title: When the replay starts, hand it back
steps.body: The memory will come back, often at night. When it does, pray one short sentence instead of rerunning the argument: *This is yours. I'm not collecting it tonight.* Then do something ordinary with your hands. You may do this dozens of times in a month, and each time counts.

moreHelp.body:
Some wounds are more than a friend or a pastor can carry with you. If what happened was abuse, assault, or another crime, you can report it, and forgiving the person never takes that choice away. The police, a victim advocate, or a lawyer can tell you what's possible where you live, even years later.

A counselor can help when the memory has taken over your sleep, your work, or your closest relationships, or when anger or fear is doing things you can't control. Your doctor can refer you, your insurance company keeps a directory, and a pastor who knows your area usually knows which counselors are trusted. If you want a Christian counselor, ask how they bring faith into their work. Whoever you see, check that they're licensed in your state and experienced with trauma, abuse, or betrayal. A good counselor won't press you to forgive or reconcile on a schedule.
signs: You're afraid of the person who hurt you, or they still have access to you or to a child.
A crime was committed against you or someone you love, whether last week or years ago.
You've had thoughts of hurting the person who hurt you, or yourself. If you're thinking about ending your life, call or text 988 now.
Memories return uninvited with panic, nightmares, or numbness, and it has gone on for weeks.
Someone is pressuring you to stay quiet, drop a report, or reconcile before you're safe.
You're under eighteen and an adult is hurting you. Tell a teacher, a school counselor, or another adult you trust.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need the right words. You can say, *I was hurt by someone close to me, and I can't get past it.* If it involved abuse or a crime, say so plainly; it tells them what kind of help you need. Then ask a few questions. Are you licensed in this state? Have you worked with people after abuse or betrayal? How do you handle a client's faith? What does a session cost, and is there a sliding scale? If the first counselor isn't a good fit, try another.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't keep you from help. Many counselors offer sliding-scale fees, and community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge much less than private practices. Your employer may offer an employee assistance program with a few free sessions, and many churches keep a benevolence fund for exactly this. If you were the victim of a crime, a victim advocate can tell you whether your state helps pay for counseling.

helping.body:
If someone tells you they can't forgive, the most important thing you can do is not hurry them; they've probably been hurried already. Believe what they tell you, let them say it without softening it, and ask whether they're safe. Your job isn't to produce forgiveness in them. It's to stay, to help them get safe if they need to, and to keep them company while God does what only he can do.

Pastors and church leaders carry a heavier duty, and we have often failed it. Don't press a victim to forgive quickly or to reconcile, and don't send anyone alone to confront the person who abused them, whatever you believe Matthew 18 requires. Never use forgiveness to protect a leader, a family's good name, or an institution. Bonhoeffer called forgiveness preached without repentance *cheap grace*; this is worse, because the victim is made to pay for it. Report abuse to the proper authorities. Mandated reporting laws may apply to you, they vary by state, and you need to know your own obligations before the day you need them. No church's reputation is worth another victim.
say: You don't have to forgive them tonight.
Forgiving them will never mean you have to go back.
I'm not going anywhere, even when you're angry.
dontSay: Think of what this will do to the church.
helping.next: Check in again next week, and the week after; the hardest days often come after everyone else has moved on. If they're in danger, help them make a safety plan with one of the hotlines above. If a child may be at risk, report it. Help them find a counselor, and offer to sit with them while they call. If they want to pray, pray a psalm with them rather than preaching at them.

prayer:
Lord, you saw what they did. I don't have to explain it to you, and I'm tired of explaining it to everyone else.

I can't forgive them. Some days I don't want to. I want them to hurt the way I've hurt, and you already know that, so I'm telling you instead of acting on it. You said vengeance belongs to you. Then take it, all of it, because I'm afraid of what I would do with it. Judge rightly. Bring the truth into the light. Protect me, and anyone else they could hurt.

I can't yet pray what your Son prayed from the cross. Teach me to want to. When the memory comes back tonight, meet me in it, and don't let this wound become the whole story of my life.

And forgive me, too, for the people I have wounded. I'm handing you the case. Keep it. Amen.

faq.q: Do I have to forgive someone who isn't sorry?
faq.a: Christians who take the Bible seriously answer this two ways, and each protects something real. One says you forgive whether or not they ever repent, pointing to Jesus' command to forgive "if you hold anything against another" (Mark 11:25) and to his prayer from the cross; it keeps you from staying chained to someone who never changes. The other says you must always be ready to forgive and must give up revenge now, but that forgiveness is completed when the offender repents: "if he repents, forgive him" (Luke 17:3). It guards against a forgiveness that skips the truth. Faithful Christians differ here; it isn't a test of faith. Both agree on what you can do tonight, which is to give up revenge and hand the case to God, and both say reconciliation waits for real repentance.

faq.q: Does forgiving mean forgetting, or letting them back in?
faq.a: No to both. The saying *forgive and forget* isn't in the Bible. When God promises that he "will remember their sins no more" (Jeremiah 31:34), he means he won't hold them against his people, not that he loses the memory. The theologian Miroslav Volf, in *The End of Memory* (2006), calls the wronged to remember rightly, truthfully and for the sake of healing and justice. Reconciliation takes two people and real change, and trust is earned slowly, if at all, so you can forgive a parent, a former spouse, or a pastor and still refuse contact and report what they did. Paul handed a man who "did great harm to me" to God's judgment and in the same breath warned Timothy, "You too should beware of him" (2 Timothy 4:14-15).

faq.q: Is it a sin to be angry at the person who hurt me?
faq.a: Anger at a real wrong isn't sin in itself. Paul writes, "Be angry, yet do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26), quoting a psalm about searching your heart on your bed at night. God is angry at injustice, and feeling nothing about abuse isn't holiness. The danger is what anger becomes when it moves in and stays: the bitterness, rage, and malice Paul tells us to get rid of a few verses later (Ephesians 4:31). Anger that goes to God, to the truth, and to protecting others can be right. Anger that settles into daydreams of revenge consumes the one who carries it.

faq.q: What does seventy times seven mean?
faq.a: Peter asked whether forgiving seven times was enough, and Jesus answered, "not just seven times, but seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:22). Older translations read seventy times seven, since the Greek can be taken either way, and the point is the same: stop counting. The number echoes Lamech, who boasted in Genesis 4:24 of being avenged seventy-sevenfold, so Jesus turns the oldest song of endless revenge into a command of endless release. With a deep wound you'll likely forgive the same thing many times, as the memory returns. That isn't proof you failed the first time. It's what forgiving a real wrong looks like.

The Bible never uses that phrase, and absolving yourself isn't the power you need. If you've wronged someone, the debt is owed to God and to the person you hurt. Confess it to God, who promises that "if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9); make amends where it's safe and possible; then accept a verdict you have no right to overrule. When your heart keeps condemning you, "God is greater than our hearts" (1 John 3:20). Refusing his forgiveness can feel like humility, but it quietly puts you back in the judge's seat. If what you carry is shame more than guilt, a pastor or counselor can help you sort it out.

faq.q: How do I forgive someone who has died?
faq.a: You forgive them without any hope of hearing them say they're sorry, which can make it harder and lonelier. Whatever you believe about forgiving someone who never repented, the part within your reach is the same: give up your claim to make them pay and hand the case to God, who now holds both them and the debt. You may be grieving two losses at once, the person and the apology that will never come. Write the letter you never got to send, read it aloud to God, and tell him you're releasing what they owed you. Where they stand before God is his to judge.

slots.note: After the paragraph on wounds made of absence: if James is willing, a few sentences in his own words on what forgiving a father who was not there has meant or cost him, or why it has been hard, and whether raising five sons changed it. The page stands without it.

After the Nietzsche paragraph: James came to faith from atheism. If he wants to, a sentence or two on how Christian forgiveness looked to him as an unbeliever and what changed his mind, only as he tells it.

The first question (forgiving someone who isn't sorry) states both views and chooses neither. James can add where he lands, the tradition behind it, and the strongest objection he has not fully answered.

sources.claim: In On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), Nietzsche argued that Christian morality grew from the resentment of the powerless, who recast their inability to take revenge as virtue, even as forgiveness, and looked to God's judgment for their vindication.
sources.cite: Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), First Essay, sections 14 and 15; summarized in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Nietzsche's Moral and Political Philosophy.

sources.claim: Miroslav Volf's The End of Memory (2006) argues for remembering wrongs rightly, truthfully and so that memory heals rather than deepens animosity.
sources.cite: Miroslav Volf, The End of Memory: Remembering Rightly in a Violent World (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2006; second edition 2021).

sources.claim: Bonhoeffer described cheap grace as the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance.
sources.cite: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship (Nachfolge, 1937), chapter 1, Costly Grace.

reviewed.notes: Writer's self-check before editorial review. Every Scripture passage and every double-quoted phrase in prose copied from node scripts/bsb.mjs and confirmed verbatim by the validator. Kit routes checked against App.tsx and the library manifests; none redirect. No statistics and no quotations of anyone but Scripture. Named thinkers limited to Nietzsche (Genealogy, 1887), Bonhoeffer (cheap grace), and Volf (The End of Memory, 2006), each confirmed by search and listed in sources. Safety before reconciliation stated in the answer, the first step, and the signs; forgiveness separated from forgetting, excusing, trust, reconciliation, contact, and silence about abuse; mandated reporting noted for pastors without legal advice. The contested question (forgiveness before repentance) is stated both ways with a slot for James. Read as the midnight reader, the skeptic, and the pastor. Needs an editor's read and James's slots before publishing.
